lesson.title: Strings Never Change: Understanding Immutability
lesson.summary: Once a string is created, none of its individual characters can be changed in place; every operation that looks like it edits a string actually builds and returns a completely new one.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to think of a string the way you might think of a list of boxes, where you could simply reach in and swap out one box for another. Python's strings do not work that way. A string is immutable, meaning that once it exists in memory, its sequence of characters is fixed for good. There is no operation that reaches into a string and changes character number 3 while leaving the rest of the string exactly as it was in the same place in memory. Every single method or operation that appears to modify a string, changing its case, replacing a substring, stripping whitespace, is actually building an entirely new string from scratch and handing that new string back to you, leaving the original completely untouched.

The clearest way to see this is to try the thing that immutability forbids. Given word = "PYTHON", attempting word[0] = "X" raises a TypeError, with a message along the lines of 'str' object does not support item assignment. This is not a bug or a missing feature; it is a deliberate design decision, and Python is telling you directly that indexing into a string can only read a character, never write one.

To actually produce a modified version of a string, you build a new string out of pieces of the old one, and reassign the variable name to point at that new string:

word = "PYTHON"
word = "X" + word[1:]
print(word)

Trace this carefully. word[1:] is a slice that takes everything from index 1 to the end of the original "PYTHON", which is "YTHON". Concatenating "X" with "YTHON" produces the brand new string "XYTHON". That new string is then assigned back to the name word, which now points at this new six-character string instead of the original one. print(word) outputs XYTHON. The original string "PYTHON" was never edited; it was simply abandoned once nothing referred to it anymore, and word was reassigned to a freshly built replacement.

This distinction between 'changing a value in place' and 'reassigning a variable to a new value' matters well beyond this one example. Every string method covered later, like .upper(), .replace(), or .strip(), follows the exact same rule: the method returns a new string, and if you want to keep that result, you must assign it to a variable, either the same one or a new one. Writing word.upper() on its own line and expecting word itself to have changed is a common and understandable mistake, and it happens specifically because of immutability.

Immutability is not just a restriction, it brings real benefits. Because a string's contents can never change after creation, Python can safely use strings as dictionary keys and store them in sets, since their value, and therefore their hash, is guaranteed never to shift underneath the program. It also means that passing a string into a function is completely safe: the function can slice it, search it, or build new strings from it, but it can never reach back and alter the original string sitting in the caller's variable, which removes an entire category of bugs that mutable data structures are prone to.
